Reading Test - Version 4

Reading Passage A

AIDS deaths blamed on immune therapy

Sylvia Hughes, Paris

THE DEATHS of three patients during trials of an experimental immune therapy for
people with AIDS have renewed controversy over experiments carried out by the French

scientist Daniel Zagury. The affair has also highlighted shortcomings in the system of
checks and controls over clinical research. *

©

The French health minister, Bruno Durieux, recently announced that an inquiry had
cleared Zagury and his team at the Pierre and Marie Curie University in Paris of alleged
irregularities in the way they conducted tests of a potential vaccine and an experimental
immune therapy in patients at the Saint-Antoine Hospital (This Week, 13 April). But
Durieux made no mention of three deaths which the inquiry had reported.

Following revelations about the circumstances in which the patients died, Durieux
has now announced a new assessment of the tests, to be undertaken by ANRS, the national
agency for AIDS research.

Last July, Zagury and his colleagues reported in a letter to The Lancet (vol 336, p
179) a trial on patients with AIDS or AIDS-related complex. The patients received a
preparation based on proteins from HIV that was designed to boost their immune systems.

The preparation was made from samples of the patients' own white blood cells,
purified and cultured in the laboratory. The researchers had infected the white blood cells
with a genetically engineered form of the vaccinia virus that had genes from HIV inserted

into its DNA. The vaccinia, or cowpox, virus, had first been inactivated with
formaldehyde, said the researchers. %

Last week, the Chicago Tribune and Le Monde alleged that at least two of the
deaths were caused by vaccinia ‘disease, a rare“complication’of infection -with vaccinia
virus. Vaccinia is harmless in healthy people and has been used in its live form as the
vaccine against smallpox worldwide. But in people whose immune systems are
suppressed, the virus can occasionally spread rapidly in the body and kill.

A Paris dermatologist, Jean-Claude Guillaume, said that when he warned Zagury's
team that he was convinced one of their patients had contracted vaccinia disease "the
response was that this was not possible" because the vaccinia had been inactivated.

Shortly before his death, the patient had consulted Guillaume about large, rubbery lesions
across his abdomen.

Guillaume consulted a colleague, Jean-Claude Roujeau, about the rare disease.
Roujeau told the Chicago Tribune that his tests on the tissue samples taken from two
patients before they died had detected vaccinia virus in their skin cells.

The Saint-Antoine team's postmortem tests did not reveal vaccinia. Odile Picard,
who is in charge of administering the treatment, says there were three possible causes of
death - vaccinia disease, herpes or a toxic reaction to the procedure used to prepare white
blood cells before injecting them into patients. Zagury, however, insisted that "nothing
allows us to affirm it [was vaccinia]. It could have been herpes or Kaposi's sarcoma".
The tests are continuing, he says. Sa

Luc Montagnier, co-discoverer of HIV, called for an immediate halt to the
experiments. He says that intravenous injections could lead to generalised vaccinia
disease. His team at the Pasteur Institute has already shown in laboratory tests that

vaccinia virus maybe dangerous if the immune system is unable to resist it.
oe al

The findings at the Pasteur Institute were apparently unknown to Zagury's team,
which works with Montagnier's rival, the researcher Robert Gallo. Gallo's collaboration
with Zagury has been suspended by the National Institutes of Health in the US because of
alleged irregularities.

Zagury and his team have also denied charges that they covered up the deaths,
which are not mentioned in their report in The Lancet. "They were not covered up," Picard
said. "They were accepted [into the trial] on compassionate grounds."

The Lancet report concerns 28 patients. 14 who were treated and 14 controls who
were not able to receive the treatment. Picard says that five other patients were also treated
with the preparation but were not compared with the controls. Their T4 cell counts had
fallen too low to be comparable with the control group, so they were excluded from the
study and not mentioned in its report.

AIDS patients are particularly vulnerable to infection. Furthermore,.the French
ethics council had specified that volunteers should be chosen because "their state was so
advanced it excluded treatment with AZT", At least some of the patients were being
treated with AZT at the same time as immune therapy.

The council had also asked to be informed of the results of the trials case by case,
but had not been told of the deaths. The geneticist André Boué, a member of the council,
said: "The ethics council does not have judicial powers; we are not the fraud squad.”

The director of the AIDS research agency ANRS. Jean-Paul Levy, is concerned
that all the controversy may lead to a crisis of public confidence but laid the blame firmly
at the door of the media where "excessive praise is followed by excessive rejection".

Levy, who had still heard nothing, "even informally" from the health ministry the
day after Durieux told parliament that ANRS would assess immune therapy trials, said he
wanted to study the problems "in depth, but not in the atmosphere of a tribunal".

ANRS has a panel of experts in therapeutic trials, which, says Levy, "might seek
international contacts to obtain a broad consensus" on the issues involved. The re search
agency's role is to carry out a purely scientific evaluation, not to assess whether there was a
breach of ethical guidelines, according to Levy.

"Tf the government called on us to examine this case, we could act very quickly,"
said Philippe Lucas of the ethics council.

Text B: Breast is best

Research into the optimal fatty acid profile of our diet continues to provide new insights. Recent studies
in infants have shown that the balance and combination of fatty acid intake may have an impact on visual
acuity and even intelligence. This provides further support for the benefits of breast-feeding and raises
questions as to the optimal fatty acid ratio of infant formula,

Human milk remains the gold standard for infant milks. It contains high levels of readily digestible
fat. In fact, about 50% of the total caloric value of human milk comes from fat. This is because fat is
a concentrated, energy source providing much needed energy in the young infant without stressing the
immature digestive system.

An adequate fat intake is crucial for development of the brain and central nervous system during the late
foetal stage and the first two years of extrauterine life. me ~

Breast milk has an optimal fatty acid profile, being a combination of monounsaturated, polyunsaturated
and saturated fatty acids. The combination and ratio of these fatty acids appears to be important in infant
development.

Crucial role

Of particular importance in breast milk is the presence of the long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids —
arachidonic acid and docosahexaenoic acid. These play crucial roles in the development of visual acuity,
the brain and the central nervous system.

Infant formula generally derives its fats from vegetable oils and therefore does not contain long-chain
polyunsaturated fatty acids. Instead, fatty acids which are their precursors are added to formula. These
are generally in the form of linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid. In the body the former is converted to
arachidonic acid while the latter is converted to docosahexaenoic acid.

In the past it has been assumed that this conversion provided all of the healthy infant’s essential fatty acid
requirements. Support for this belief was based on the fact that infants receiving formulas containing only
linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid exhibited adequate growth rates. However, recent studies of both
premature and full-term infants have questioned this assumption.

There is a high concentration of docosahexaenoic acid in retinal and neural tissues. Studies in pre-term
infants show that infants fed with an infant formula have lowered visual acuity when compared with breast-
fed infants. Breast-fed premature infants have also been shown to have higher levels of docosahexaenoic
acid in the retina (Uauy R D et al, Ped Research, 1990; 28:485-492).

When docosahexaenoic acid was added to the diets of the formula-fed infants via a supplement with fish
oil, the concentration of docosahexaenoic acid improved, as did visual response.

Australian studies on full-term infants have confirmed these findings. Breast-fed babies have higher levels
of docosahexaenoic acid and perform better on visual acuity tests than formula-fed infants (Clark K J
et al, J Ped, 1992; 120:S151-158). There is a positive correlation between erythrocyte docosahexaenoic
acid and visual acuity.

Implications

Although the long-term implications of these findings are uriclear, they suggest that infant formulas
containing only linoleic and alpha-linolenic acid may not be effective at meeting the full essential fatty
acid requirements of healthy infants.

Breast-feeding may also affect intelligence. In a UK study, pre-term infants in an intensive care unit were
tube-fed either breast milk or an infant formula for a period of four weeks.

These infants were then followed up at seven years of age when testing was undertaken. Infants who had
been breast-fed scored on average 7-8 points higher on IQ scores than those fed with formula.

While the relationship between IQ and the level of docosahexaenoic acid remains unclear, this area is
receiving close attention.

Both the combination and ratio of fatty acid in milks are important. There are now infant formulas
available which possess a ratio of arachidonic acid to alpha-linolenic acid comparable to that of breast
milk. However, even infant formulas with a high linoleic acid to alpha-linolenic acid ratio do not result in
tissue levels of arachidonic acid as high as those found in breast-fed infants (Clark K J et al, J Ped, 1992;
120:S151-158).

Challenge

The challenge for the pharmaceutical industry is to devise new blends that result in tissue levels of
arachidonic and docosahexaenoic acid similar to those found in breast-fed infants.

This has been attempted by adding fish oil and egg, but trials studying this are inconclusive.
